newsitem.title: USA: Triumphant Clinton returns to revamp Cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Triumphant Clinton returns to revamp Cabinet.

text.p: A triumphant President Bill Clinton returned to the White House on Wednesday to plan a new administration after four Cabinet members, including his secretaries of state and defence, decided to resign.

Flush with his victory over Republican Bob Dole, Clinton flew to Washington from Little Rock, Arkansas, his home state, where he spent the night after becoming the first Democrat to win re-election to the White House in more than 50 years.
Clinton held a rally on the White House South Lawn with several hundred key officials, at times joking lightheartedly but also saying much work remains to be done.

"Very often I get the credit for the work you do and when something goes haywire, if I make a mistake, you have to figure out how to clean it up," Clinton said. "I appreciate that and I'm sure I'll give you other opportunities.

"We have a lot more hard work to do, but when our work is done and when there is eight years of sustained, disciplined effort, we will have gone a long way toward preparing our country for this new century," he added.

Officials said Clinton had already turned his mind to his first challenge, rearranging his Cabinet. They said two top aides -- Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Defence Secretary William Perry -- had told him they would resign.
One official also said Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor was making plans to return to private life, while another reported that Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary would leave.
Christopher, 71, and Perry, 69, were pillars of Clinton's national security policy.
Officials said Christopher was expected to keep his post until Clinton's inauguration on Jan. 20.
They said Perry had told Clinton he planned to resign and may return to private life within a few months once a successor is chosen.

U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright and former Senator George Mitchell are considered leading candidates to succeed Christopher, while there has been much speculation that CIA Director John Deutch may take Perry's place.

Officials said Clinton planned to meet with his Cabinet to discuss the changes on Friday. A news conference to unveil the departures, though not necessarily their replacements, was expected to be held soon.

Although officials say there is no deadline, several have said Clinton would like to announce some decisions before Tuesday, when he is scheduled to begin a vacation in Hawaii, followed by visits to the Philippines, Australia and Thailand.

Another key appointment -- a replacement for White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta -- is also in the offing and White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters Clinton had put in the most work on selecting candidates for this crucial job.

On Tuesday Panetta suggested Clinton might offer some Cabinet jobs to Republicans. "It is going to be based, hopefully, on those who are best qualified to serve in those positions, and that could include some Republicans," he said.

Americans sent a mixed message to politicians in Tuesday's election, re-electing Clinton by 49.2 percent of the vote to Dole's 40.8 percent, with over 99 percent of ballots counted, while leaving both houses of Congress in Republican hands.

Talking with reporters on Air Force One, Clinton signalled that he wants to reach out to the Republicans, with whom he collaborated on a string of new laws in the final six weeks of the Congressional term.
"If we can somehow recreate for the next four years the spirit that prevailed in the last six weeks of the Congress, we can do great things," Clinton said.
"If we can apply that spirit to balancing the budget, to education reform, to moving people from welfare to work ... we are going to have a great, great opportunity here," he added.
